control_name: Encryption of Data at Rest and Cryptographic Key Management
objective: Reduce the value of physical or storage-layer access to protected information by rendering stored data unreadable without a key, and keep the keys themselves under controlled, attributable custody.
description: Protected information at rest — primary datastores, object storage, backups, snapshots, and log archives — is encrypted using a documented algorithm and key length. Keys are held in a managed key service, access to key material is restricted to a defined set of principals, key use is logged, and rotation follows a defined schedule. Encryption is enforced at the platform level so that new storage inherits it by default rather than depending on per-resource configuration.
owner_role: Platform Engineering, with Security Engineering accountable for key policy

conditions: Protected information is persisted to storage the entity controls or contracts for
not_applicable_when: No protected information is persisted within the system boundary; transient in-memory processing only

implementation_guidance: Enforce encryption as a platform default or organisation policy, so an engineer cannot create unencrypted storage rather than merely being asked not to.
Decide and document whether provider-managed or customer-managed keys are used, and be able to explain why; both are defensible, silence is not.
Restrict key administration separately from key use. The ability to decrypt and the ability to delete or export a key are different privileges.
Ensure backups, snapshots, and replicas inherit encryption. These are the objects most often left unencrypted while the primary datastore is compliant.
Log key use and make the log part of the evidence package; an encryption setting alone says nothing about who could decrypt.
Define a rotation cadence you will actually meet, and treat rotation failures as tracked exceptions rather than silent drift.
design_considerations: Does enforcement cover every storage class holding protected information, including backups and derived copies?
Is key administration segregated from the population that routinely reads data?
Would a compromise of the application layer also yield the keys, and if so what does the control actually mitigate?
operating_considerations: Was encryption enforced for the full period, or introduced partway through?
Were any resources created unencrypted during the period, and how would the organization know?
Did key rotation occur on the stated cadence, and were exceptions authorised?

evidence_examples.note: Encryption settings and key policy across in-scope storage.
Converts point-in-time encryption state into period coverage.

risks.description: Storage-layer or backup media access yields readable protected information.
Key custody is broad enough that encryption provides no meaningful separation from a compromised application identity.

related_controls.note: Cryptographic erasure is only a valid sanitization method where key custody is controlled.
At-rest and in-transit protection are commonly governed by the same policy but tested separately.

source_refs.supports: Identity of the criterion this control is intended to help meet.
Design and operating considerations, and the points most commonly challenged in testing.
Implementation guidance and DriftGuard's recommended approach.

notes: Encryption at rest is not named as a required control by the criteria. CC6.1 states an objective about logical access security over protected information assets; encryption is a common way to help meet it.
Mapped secondarily to CC6.5 because cryptographic erasure depends on this control, and to CC6.7 because the same key management governs data in motion.
